overview: This file concerns aviation facilities in Japanese-ruled Taiwan, combining administrative cross-references, U.S. consular reporting, a landing-field map, and translations of official colonial notices. It includes a 1943 cross-reference to intelligence on additional Formosan air bases obtained from members of the Taiwan Revolutionary League in Chungking; records of Richard Halliburton and Moye W. Stephens’s proposed 1932 flight over Taiwan; and detailed reports on public aviation grounds established at Taihoku in 1935 and Giran in 1936. Collectively, the documents show American interest in Taiwan’s aviation infrastructure, Japanese sensitivity about inquiries into airfields, and the relationship between nominally public facilities, restrictions on foreign aircraft, and wider military concerns.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Chungking despatch on Formosan air bases
subfiles.to: Atchison, as recorded on the sheet
subfiles.about: This sheet directs researchers to Despatch No. 1374 concerning additional air bases in Formosa and a list of the island’s airfields.
subfiles.summary: The referenced material was a translation of a document obtained from Formosans in Chungking associated with the Taiwan Revolutionary League. It reportedly listed airfields in Formosa and supplied information about each. The sheet directs the reader to file 894a.20/15; the OCR date “1953” has been treated as an apparent misreading of 1943.

subfiles.title: File note directing readers to Franklin’s Report No. 47
subfiles.about: This filing note points to another decimal-file location for Lynn W. Franklin’s report on the proposed Stephens-Halliburton flight and its Taiwan landing-field map.
subfiles.summary: The note directs readers to file 800.79611-Halliburton, Richard/35 for Report No. 47 from Amoy. It identifies the subject as the proposed flight of Stephens and Halliburton over Taiwan and a map supplied by the Japanese Consul at Amoy. The mapped military drill ground had been prepared as a temporary landing field for the fliers.

subfiles.title: Franklin’s report on the proposed flight to Taiwan
subfiles.from: Lynn W. Franklin, American Consul at Amoy
subfiles.to: Nelson Trusler Johnson, American Minister at Peiping
subfiles.about: Franklin reports on a proposed Taiwan flight by Stephens and Halliburton and transmits a map of a temporary landing field supplied by the Japanese consul.
subfiles.summary: Franklin encloses a copy of a map showing a military drill ground prepared as a temporary landing field specifically for Stephens and Halliburton. The Japanese Consul at Amoy had subsequently received word that the proposed flight would not take place. Franklin also gave a copy of the map to the commander of the USS Stewart, who reportedly forwarded it to the Commander-in-Chief of the U.S. Asiatic Fleet.

subfiles.title: Map of a landing field in Formosa
subfiles.from: Japanese Consul at Amoy (source of the map)
subfiles.to: Moye W. Stephens and Richard Halliburton (intended users)
subfiles.about: This enclosure is a map or plan of the temporary Formosan landing field prepared for the proposed flight.
subfiles.summary: The surviving OCR identifies the image only as “Landing Field - Formosa.” The accompanying despatch explains that it depicts a military drill ground adapted as a temporary landing field. The Japanese Consul at Amoy supplied the map for Stephens and Halliburton’s use.

subfiles.title: Maney’s despatch on the new Taihoku aviation field
subfiles.about: Maney transmits an official notice establishing a new public aviation field at Taihoku.
subfiles.summary: Maney encloses a translation of a notice published in the Taiwan Government-General’s Official Gazette on September 24, 1935. He explains that further investigation would be politically unwise because local military authorities regarded inquiries about aviation fields with suspicion. Copies were also sent to the U.S. Embassy and Consulate General in Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Official notice establishing Taihoku Aviation Ground
subfiles.from: Kenzo Nakagawa, Governor General of Taiwan
subfiles.about: The translated notice announces the establishment and specifications of the state-owned Taihoku Aviation Ground at Matsuyama-sho.
subfiles.summary: Notice No. 131 establishes Taihoku Aviation Ground for public use from September 25, 1935, with the state both operating and owning it. The notice locates the field at Matsuyama-sho in Shichisei-gun, gives coordinates, and describes a level 469,421-square-meter site with an approximately 900-by-700-meter landing field. It records generally easterly winds and a signal post, while an added note places the field about three miles northeast of Taihoku Railway Station.

subfiles.title: Maney’s despatch on the new Giran aviation field
subfiles.about: Maney transmits an official notice inaugurating a public aviation field at Giran on Taiwan’s northeastern coast.
subfiles.summary: The despatch encloses a translation of Notice No. 111 from the Taiwan Government-General’s Official Gazette of July 14, 1936. Maney notes that Giran was not a port of entry for foreign trade. Aircraft arriving directly from abroad would consequently not be permitted to use the new field.

subfiles.title: Official notice establishing Giran Aviation Ground
subfiles.from: Kenzo Nakagawa, Governor General of Taiwan
subfiles.about: The translated notice records the establishment, ownership, layout, facilities, and operating period of Giran Aviation Ground.
subfiles.summary: Notice No. 111 states that Giran Aviation Ground was established as of July 13, 1936, for public use and operated by the Town of Giran. Its land was held by several public bodies, including the state, the town, the Giran Irrigation Association, and the Taihoku Provincial Agricultural Association. The notice describes a flat, T-shaped runway area extending 800 meters in each principal direction, prevailing northeasterly winds, a signal post and airfield sign, and an authorized period ending June 30, 1946.

interest: The file is valuable for the unusually precise technical and administrative information preserved in its translated colonial notices, including coordinates, dimensions, wind directions, facilities, land ownership, and authorization periods. It also connects civilian aviation with military intelligence: a field prepared for celebrity travelers was circulated to the U.S. Asiatic Fleet, while an American consul later avoided direct investigation because of Japanese military suspicion. The Chungking cross-reference further links Taiwan’s airfield network to wartime intelligence supplied by Formosan anti-Japanese activists, making the bundle useful for studying aviation, surveillance, colonial government, and Taiwanese resistance together.
